alphabet-and-sounds.explanationHtml:
The English Alphabet (26 Letters)

English uses the Latin alphabet. There are 5 vowels (A, E, I, O, U) and 21 consonants.

Vowels can make short sounds (like cat, bed, sit) or long sounds (like cake, meat, time).

basic-greetings.title: Basic Greetings & Hello
basic-greetings.description: Essential greetings: Hello, Good morning, How are you?, and Goodbye.
basic-greetings.objectivesJson: ["Greet someone politely","Ask how someone is doing","Say farewell properly"]
basic-greetings.explanationHtml:
Saying Hello & Goodbye

Greetings change based on the time of day and formality.

  • Morning (until 12:00 PM): Good morning!
  • Afternoon (12:00 PM - 5:00 PM): Good afternoon!
  • Evening (after 5:00 PM): Good evening!
  • Casual (anytime): Hi! or Hello!

present-simple-routines.description: Express habits, daily routines, and master the third-person -s rule.
present-simple-routines.objectivesJson: ["Describe your daily schedule","Apply the third-person -s correctly","Form negative sentences with don't/doesn't"]
present-simple-routines.explanationHtml:
Present Simple Tense

Use Present Simple for habits, routines, and permanent facts.

Rule: With He, She, It, add -s or -es to the verb!

Example: "I drink coffee every morning, but she drinks tea."

The Past Simple Tense

professional-presentation.title: Professional Presentation & Persuasion
professional-presentation.description: Techniques for captivating international audiences, handling tough questions, and signposting.
professional-presentation.objectivesJson: ["Master signposting language for presentations","Handle difficult client inquiries politely","Persuade stakeholders using evidence"]
professional-presentation.explanationHtml:
Signposting in Business Presentations

Signposts are phrases that guide your listeners through your presentation structure.

  • Starting: "Today I would like to walk you through our Q3 expansion roadmap..."
  • Transitioning: "Now let's turn our attention to the financial projections..."
  • Concluding: "To sum up, three key factors will drive our growth..."
professional-presentation.examplesJson: [{"phrase":"Let us examine the data from another perspective.","translation":"Examinemos los datos desde otra perspectiva.","note":"Analytical transition"},{"phrase":"In light of recent market trends, we recommend a proactive strategy.","translation":"A la luz de las tendencias recientes del mercado, recomendamos una estrategia proactiva.","note":"Executive recommendation"}]

exercises.prompt: Which signposting phrase is best for moving to the next presentation topic?
exercises.optionsJson: ["Moving on to our next agenda item...","I am done with that now.","Stop listening to what I just said.","Next thing I guess."]
exercises.correctAnswer: Moving on to our next agenda item...
exercises.explanation: "Moving on to..." is professional, courteous, and clear signposting.

inversion-and-emphasis.title: Subtle Inversion & Rhetorical Emphasis
inversion-and-emphasis.description: Use negative inversions (Rarely have I seen..., Not only did she...) for dramatic and formal emphasis.
inversion-and-emphasis.objectivesJson: ["Master negative inversions with rarely, seldom, hardly","Elevate academic essays and executive memos","Avoid common inversion word-order mistakes"]
inversion-and-emphasis.explanationHtml:
Negative Inversion for High-Level English

In formal English, when a sentence begins with a restrictive or negative word (Rarely, Seldom, Never, Not only, Under no circumstances), the subject and auxiliary verb invert, exactly like a question!

Standard: I have rarely witnessed such dedication.
Inverted: Rarely have I witnessed such dedication.

idiomatic-mastery-subtext.explanationHtml:
The Zenith of Fluency: Idiomatic Precision

C2 English is characterized not just by grammatical perfection, but by an instinctive grasp of cadence, cultural resonance, and subtle understatement.

When a native speaker says "It was not entirely without merit," they mean it possessed some value, employing litotes (understatement by double negative).

a0-survival-greetings.explanationHtml:
Saying Hello & Goodbye

Greetings change based on the time of day:

  • Morning (before 12 PM): Good morning!
  • Afternoon (12 PM - 5 PM): Good afternoon!
  • Evening (after 5 PM): Good evening!
  • Anytime casual: Hi! or Hello!

Numbers & Telling Time

To ask the time: "What time is it?"

c1-diplomatic-hedging-tact.title: Diplomatic Nuance, Hedging & Subtle Tactfulness
c1-diplomatic-hedging-tact.description: Soften absolute statements using modal hedges, epistemic verbs (tend to, seem to), and tactful euphemisms.
c1-diplomatic-hedging-tact.objectivesJson: ["Avoid overly dogmatic assertions in professional communication","Deploy hedges (arguably, conceivably, it appears that)","Disagree diplomatically without causing offense"]
c1-diplomatic-hedging-tact.explanationHtml:
The Art of Hedging in English

In executive leadership and diplomacy, bald assertions sound aggressive. Hedging introduces nuance and scientific caution:

Bald: "Your forecast is wrong."

Hedged: "It appears that certain underlying assumptions in the forecast might warrant further scrutiny."

Understatement & Cultural Irony

In native English culture, especially British and American, intense praise is often disguised as mild understatement:

"That presentation wasn't half bad!" = It was extraordinary and brilliant.

Litotes is the deliberate use of understatement in which an affirmative is expressed by the negative of its contrary:

c2-legal-contractual-syntax.explanationHtml:
Contractual Register & Legalese

In high-level international law and finance, terms carry precise statutory meaning:

  • Pursuant to: In accordance with ("Pursuant to Clause 14...")
  • Indemnification: Compensation for harm or loss.
  • Notwithstanding the foregoing: Irrespective of what was just stated.

u7-l1-professional-emails.title: Writing Clear Professional Emails
u7-l1-professional-emails.description: Subject lines, formal openings, requesting updates, and polite sign-offs.

Close with "Best regards," or "Sincerely,".

u7-l2-meetings-opinions.title: Meetings & Expressing Opinions Diplomatically
u7-l2-meetings-opinions.description: Agreeing, politely disagreeing, interrupting tactfully, and summarizing.
u7-l2-meetings-opinions.objectivesJson: ["Disagree politely without sounding rude","Introduce your perspective with \"In my view\""]
u7-l2-meetings-opinions.explanationHtml:
Diplomatic Disagreement

Instead of saying "You are wrong", native speakers say:
"I see your point, but from my perspective..."

u9-l1-negative-inversion.title: Negative Inversion for Rhetorical Impact
u9-l1-negative-inversion.description: Hardly had, Seldom do, Not only... but also, Under no circumstances.
u9-l1-negative-inversion.objectivesJson: ["Master inverted syntax for emphatic emphasis","Analyze formal literary and oratorical prose"]
u9-l1-negative-inversion.explanationHtml:
Negative Inversion

When negative or limiting adverbs start a sentence, invert the subject and auxiliary verb:
"Never have I seen such dedication." (Instead of "I have never seen...")
u9-l1-negative-inversion.examplesJson: [{"phrase":"Seldom do we encounter such remarkable eloquence.","translation":"Raras veces nos encontramos con una elocuencia tan notable.","note":"Inversion with seldom"},{"phrase":"Not only did they meet the target, but they surpassed it.","translation":"No solo cumplieron la meta, sino que la superaron.","note":"Emphatic correlation"}]
